newsitem.title: BELARUS: WORLD BANK TO RESUME BELARUS LOANS IF IT REFORMS.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BANK TO RESUME BELARUS LOANS IF IT REFORMS.

text.p: The World Bank is ready to resume funding to Belarus and may sign a loan memorandum soon, providing the former Soviet republic meets economic reform conditions, a bank representative said on Wednesday.
"The World Bank is ready to re-open credits if the government fulfils its obligations," director Basil Kavalsky told a news conference after meeting senior officials.

He said if Belarus renewed a macroeconomic reform programme with the International Monetary Fund (IMF), which froze a standby credit of $300 million a year ago, World Bank credits could be up to $100 million annually.
A $30 to 40 million loan to support small business development would be available more immediately, Kavalsky said.
"I think it's well known we would like to see reform take place more rapidly in Belarus," he said. The main need is to speed up privatisation in the country of 10 million people, he added.

Although he said Belarus had met certain conditions last month by accelerating small-scale privatisation, implementing bankruptcy laws, and loosening money market regulations, he warned it would have to do more to prove itself.
"If there continues to be such a discrepancy between actions and words it will continue to be impossible for us to provide support," Kavalsky said.
President Alexander Lukashenko maintains tight control of the economy, fixing prices, controlling the central bank and demanding the economy perform according to his economic plan, effective to 2000.

Inflation has picked up sharply in recent weeks, doubling to a monthly rate of 13.3 percent in January. Monetary policy has also concerned economists since the official rate of the Belarussian rouble in Minsk varies greatly from the Moscow rate.
The World Bank had disbursed $115 million of $170 million in promised credits before halting payments last May.
Kavalsky said the Belarus government was stepping up reforms following a depletion in currency reserves, acceleration in inflation, and deterioration in relations with Russia last year.
IMF officials visiting Minsk last week said they were not considering reopening the standby credit.
